enrichment.short_title: Auditor share valuation negligence and margin of error
key_facts: David Goldstein sold his Marchday Group plc shares at a price fixed by the company's auditors, Levy Gee partner Julian Synett, under article 14 of the articles of association.

Synett instructed property valuers to value the portfolio as a single transaction, deducted full contingent tax on investment properties, applied a 12.5% unlisted-company discount, and assumed 75% exercise of directors' share options.
Goldstein alleged negligent valuation; expert Tony Hindley valued the shares materially higher.
The trial turned on whether negligence could be established where the final figure fell within an acceptable valuation bracket.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Chancery trial of a professional negligence claim against auditors who certified the prescribed price for compulsory share purchase under the company's articles.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed: Synett's certified value fell within the permissible bracket once corrected variables were applied, so under Merivale Moore plc v Strutt & Parker no liability arose despite identifiable process errors.
enrichment.ratio: In negligent valuation claims where the complaint relates to the figures in a valuation, a figure outside the permissible margin of error is a necessary precondition of liability; process errors that do not move the final figure outside the bracket do not sound in damages, consistently with the ratio of Merivale Moore.
legal_issues: Process versus outcome in professional valuer negligence
Application of the margin of error or bracket approach
Reconciliation of Lion Nathan, SAAMCO, and Merivale Moore authorities
Proper basis for valuing property-company shares under articles requiring willing buyer/willing seller valuation
Whether contingent tax and portfolio discounts were negligently applied

enrichment.short_title: Observer libel article held to be comment not fact
key_facts: Sara Keays brought libel proceedings over Carol Sarler's Observer comment piece criticising her media campaign with her daughter Flora after Flora turned 18.
Flora Keays, Lord Parkinson's daughter, had been subject to long-standing publicity restrictions during childhood.
Keays claimed the article bore meanings including cynical exploitation of Flora, lying about inevitable publicity, and a revenge-motivated kiss-and-tell to The Times.
The defendants applied for a ruling that the words were incapable of being factual and were comment only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim Queen's Bench application in libel proceedings to determine whether the complained-of words are only capable of being regarded as comment rather than fact.
enrichment.outcome: Application upheld: a jury would be perverse to treat the defamatory imputations as factual statements requiring justification rather than comment defended as fair comment on a matter of public interest.
enrichment.ratio: Where a journalist in a comment section draws inferences about a person's motives from publicly available media coverage, especially states of mind that cannot be verified, reasonable readers will treat the imputations as opinion or value judgment rather than objective fact.

Whether allegations of lying and motive are capable of being comment
Application of Branson v Bower and Kemsley v Foot principles

enrichment.short_title: Wasted costs order against estate solicitors reversed
key_facts: Claudia Sherman challenged Len Woolnough's 1993 will after he left his Brighton house to charities instead of the family.
Executrix Mrs Perkins, advised by Fitzhugh Gates, issued an originating summons seeking an inquiry into Claudia's interest after years of threatened but unissued probate challenges.
Master Moncaster held severance had occurred and ordered costs from the sale proceeds; a deputy judge later made a wasted costs order against the solicitors on indemnity basis.
The judge criticised the proceedings' form, failure to notify Claudia of the Master's views, and conflict of interest between Emma's and Len's estates.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against a deputy High Court judge's wasted costs order made on a late appeal from a costs order in estate proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed: Master's costs order restored; wasted costs and indemnity costs orders set aside; interim payments ordered by the deputy judge to be repaid.
enrichment.ratio: A wasted costs order requires improper, unreasonable or negligent conduct causing unnecessary costs and that it is just to compensate the applicant; solicitors who reasonably brought proceedings to resolve a beneficiary's prolonged vacillation, acting on counsel's advice, are not liable even if procedural form was imperfect.

Appropriate procedure where a will is proved in common form but challenged

enrichment.short_title: Real possibility test for uncertain perpetrators in care cases
key_facts: Eleven-week-old M suffered serious non-accidental injuries on two occasions, including fractures, retinal and subdural haemorrhages, and brain damage.
Care proceedings used a split trial; Charles J found threshold met but applied a 'no possibility' test and left parents, grandmother and night nanny in the pool of possible perpetrators.
The night nanny had not been a party at first instance; the grandmother was joined for the appeal.
All parties agreed the judge's perpetrator test was wrong following Re O and N; Re B.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal in public law care proceedings following the threshold stage of a split trial on identification of perpetrators of non-accidental injury.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed: 'no possibility' test rejected; night nanny and maternal grandmother excluded as possible perpetrators; real possibility remains that one or both parents caused the injuries.
enrichment.ratio: Where the court cannot identify a perpetrator on the balance of probabilities, it should ask whether there is a real possibility or likelihood that a named carer was the perpetrator; exculpation requires absence of real possibility, not merely some theoretical opportunity.
legal_issues: Correct test for identifying possible perpetrators of inflicted injury
Relationship between threshold findings and welfare stage in split trials
Procedural fairness to non-parties such as the night nanny and grandmother
Interpretation of section 31(2)(b) in shared-care cases
Effect of Lancashire County Council v B and Re O and N; Re B

enrichment.short_title: No Court of Appeal jurisdiction on licensing case stated
key_facts: Westminster licensing magistrates had granted a Special Hours Certificate for part of on-licence premises without a music and dancing licence.

enrichment.short_title: Nightclub owner vicariously liable for doorman's stabbing
key_facts: Doorman Stephen Cranston, employed at Flamingo's nightclub in Woolwich, stabbed David Mattis in the back after an earlier violent ejection incident in the club.
Cranston left the club, armed himself at his flat, returned and stabbed Mattis who had briefly intervened to protect another customer.
Owner Gerard Pollock knew Cranston was unlicensed, aggressive and used as an intimidatory bouncer.
The trial judge held the stabbing was a separate incident after Cranston left employment and dismissed the claim.

enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on vicarious liability and personal duty; leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: An employer may be vicariously liable for a doorman's deliberate knife attack outside the club where the assault was closely connected to aggressive door supervision the employer authorised and expected, motivated by revenge for humiliation arising from the earlier incident at work.

enrichment.short_title: Conviction quashed after informant witness lied on oath
key_facts: Martindale was convicted of conspiring with Adrian Payne to supply heroin between September 1995 and January 1996.
Payne, the principal prosecution witness, denied under oath that he was a police informant or had received police money.
After trial it emerged Payne was a registered informant who had received an expenses payment and been recommended for incentive payment; this was not disclosed.
Police policy prevented passing informant status to the CPS; the judge summing up reinforced Payne's denials.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission treated as an appeal against conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed as unsafe; Crown indicated no retrial.
enrichment.ratio: A conviction is unsafe where a central accomplice witness lied on oath about being a police informant and receiving payments, and that material was not disclosed so the defence could not undermine his credibility at trial.
legal_issues: Effect of non-disclosure of witness informant status

Whether other police evidence could sustain conspiracy without Payne
Application of Pendleton fresh evidence test

enrichment.short_title: Broker negligence claim not estopped by coverage trial
key_facts: KUCC and RTZ group companies lost cover for smelter modernisation plant after explosions in 1995 because FCF and acid plant had not met operational attachment requirements.

enrichment.short_title: Rent assessment committee reduction upheld on appeal

statutes_considered.title: Rent Assessment Committees (England and Wales) Regulations 1971

key_facts: Park Lane Properties let a five-bedroom Leeds student flat at £58.50 per person per week under an assured shorthold tenancy from July 2002.
Five tenants applied under section 22 Housing Act 1988 for a rent assessment.
The Northern Rent Assessment Committee inspected the property and reduced rent to £52.50 per week, finding the charged rent more than 10% above the reasonable market rent.
The landlord appealed on alleged misunderstanding of comparables, improper use of local knowledge, procedural unfairness and inadequate reasons.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on a point of law under section 11 Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 from a Rent Assessment Committee determination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; committee decision upheld; landlord ordered to pay respondent's costs of £4,437.50 within 28 days.
enrichment.ratio: A rent assessment committee may properly rely on its members' local market knowledge together with the evidence before it when fixing the rent a landlord might reasonably expect under section 22(3), provided it considers the totality of comparables and gives reasons showing how it reached the figure.

Whether advertised comparables for a future academic year were properly treated
Significance threshold under section 22(3)(b)
Adequacy of reasons for a more than 10% reduction
Procedural fairness when challenging selective landlord comparables
